title: The Link between Culture and Thought

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For more than a century, Western philosophers and psychologists have based their discussions of thought patterns on one basic principle: that the Tibet or the grasslands of Africa. Cultural differences might determine what same processes underlie all human thought. The people think about: teenage boys in remote areas of Africa, for instance, strategies people adopt in processing information and making sense of the world around them are, Western scholars have assumed, the same for everyone.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: However, recent research by Dr Richard Nisbett, a social psychologist at the conducted a number of studies with various colleagues comparing groups of University of Michigan, has challenged this long-held view. Dr Nisbett Americans of European descent (representing ‘Westerners') with groups from various East Asian countries (representing ‘Easterners'). They found that people who belong to different cultures do not just think about different things: their elementary thought processes are different. Actually, these researchers were not the first to propose that thought processes may vary in differing cultures. For example, psychologists in the Soviet Union in the 1930s conducted research into how farmers solved problems of logic, to find out if their intellectual processes were affected by their environment. But the University of Michigan work has been of particular interest in academic circles because it tried to define and elaborate on cultural differences through a series of tightly controlled, empirical laboratory experiments. In the broadest sense the Michigan studies, carried out in the United States, Japan, China and Korea, document a basic contrast between East and West, and in doing so they raise questions about the assumptions of cognitive psychology that have been made for the past half a century.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In one of the studies, conducted by Dr Nisbett and Takahiko Masuda, subjects from Japan and from the United States were shown an animated video of an underwater situation, in which one very large fish swam among smaller fish and other aquatic features. Asked to describe what they saw, the Japanese (or Eastern) subjects were likely to begin by talking about the scene. They might say, for example, 'The bottom was rocky'. The American (or Western) subjects tended to begin their descriptions with the largest fish, making statements like 'There was a huge fish swimming to the right'. Overall, the Japanese made 70 per cent more statements about the background environment than the Americans, and twice as many statements about the relationships between the fish and their context. A Japanese subject might note, for example, that 'The big fish swam past the seaweed'. And, the greater attention paid by the Easterners to context and relationship was more than just superficial. Shown another video of the same large fish swimming in a different environment, the Japanese participants had more difficulty than the American subjects in recognizing that it was the same fish. This indicated that the perception of the Japanese was closely dependent upon what they saw in the background.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: In another study, Dr Nisbett and Incheol Choi found that Easterners were more likely than Westerners to appreciate both sides of an argument. The researchers presented groups of Koreans and Americans with very convincing arguments in support of a particular position. Both the Koreans and the Americans at first expressed strong support for that position. However, when the groups were then presented with arguments opposing the initial position, the Korean subjects generally modified and decreased their support for that first position, while the Americans actually increased their original support.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In yet another study, again focusing on Americans and Koreans, Dr Nisbett and Ara Norenzayan found indications that when logic and fact do not agree, Westerners are more likely than Easterners to stick to the rules of formal logic. For example, the subjects were presented with a logical sequence like: 'All animals with fur hibernate. Rabbits have fur. Therefore rabbits hibernate'. The Americans were more likely to accept the validity of the series of statements. They assumed the conclusion must be true because of the logical structure of the argument. The Korean subjects, by contrast, more frequently judged the argument as invalid based on their own understanding that it was not actually true - not all animals with fur do, of course, hibernate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: While the cultural differences traced in the Michigan research are substantial, their origins are much less clear. Historical evidence suggests that a divide between Oriental and Occidental thinking has existed since ancient times. How much of this is a result of variations in language, religious practices or even geography is anyone's guess. Both styles, Dr Nisbett says, have advantages and limitations, and neither is written into the genes; many Asian-Americans are indistinguishable in their modes of thought from European-Americans. Anthropologist Dr Alan Fiske says, 'In my field we describe the way these different groups talk and interact. But these descriptions are qualitative in nature rather than being controlled as an experiment would be, so Dr Nisbett's research is a valuable complement to our work'. Yet not everyone agrees that all Dr Nisbett's findings reflect fundamental differences. Psychologist Dr Patricia Cheng finds some of the findings matched her personal experience. But she says, 'I think that some differences - the Asian tolerance for contradiction, for example - are purely social'. Still, to the extent that the studies reflect real differences in perception, psychologists may have to develop models of mental processes that take cultural influences into account.
